anomalies.observed: The GND1 and GND2 pins of both isolated CAN transceivers (U10, U11) are connected to the same GND net.
anomalies.expected: Isolated CAN transceivers require separate grounds (GND1 and GND2) to maintain galvanic isolation, as specified.

evidence.quote: GND [High Power] : ... U10.4(GND1,power_in) U10.5(GND2,power_in) U11.4(GND1,power_in) U11.5(GND2,power_in) ...
two isolated CAN buses (CAN0, CAN1), each driven by its own MCP2515 SPI CAN controller (U8, U9) through an isolated CAN transceiver (U11/companion)

anomalies.impact: Loss of galvanic isolation between the CAN buses and the rest of the board, defeating the intended isolation and risking ground loops or damage to the CM4.

anomalies.observed: The OE pin of the TXS0101 level shifter (U7) is tied to GND.
anomalies.expected: The OE pin of a TXS0101 is active high and must be tied high (e.g., to VCCA) to enable the level shifter.
anomalies.impact: The level shifter is permanently disabled, so the WS2812 data from Module1.GPIO13 cannot reach D5.DIN, and the addressable LEDs D5-D7 and D18-D21 will not function.

anomalies.observed: The anodes of LEDs D8, D28, and D29 are connected to GND.
anomalies.expected: LED anodes should be connected to a positive supply (e.g., +3V3) so they can forward bias when their cathodes are pulled low.
anomalies.impact: These LEDs will never illuminate, so the intended e-stop status indication is lost.

parsed.summary: The design files contain multiple anomalies: the isolated CAN transceivers have their grounds tied together, defeating isolation; the WS2812 level shifter U7 is disabled by tying its OE pin to GND; and three e-stop indicator LEDs have their anodes grounded, so they can never light.

This is typical for LTC4412: VIN is input, SENSE is output, GATE drives P-MOSFET. But wait, LTC4412 is a PowerPath controller for load sharing between a wall adapter and battery. Actually for P-channel, to turn on, gate must be lower than source. If source is at VIN, drain at load, then when on, current flows from VIN to load. In netlist, Q1.2 S is +5V (load), Q1.3 D is USBC_VBUS_IN (input). So source is on load side, drain on input side. That means the P-MOSFET is reversed. Let's analyze: LTC4412 GATE drives gate low to turn on P-MOSFET. For P-MOS, turn on when Vgs < Vth (negative). If source is +5V and drain is VBUS, then when VBUS > +5V, Vgs = Vg - 5V. If gate is pulled low (0V), Vgs = -5V, so it turns on, connecting VBUS to +5V. That works. But the body diode: for P-MOS, body diode is from drain to source (anode drain, cathode source). So if VBUS > +5V, body diode conducts from VBUS to +5V. So it works. If VBUS < +5V, body diode blocks. So it's actually correct for reverse current protection? The LTC4412 senses output +5V and controls gate to regulate. The source is on output, drain on input. That is a common configuration for ideal diode: P-MOSFET with source at output, drain at input, so body diode conducts from input to output. Yes, for ideal diode, you want body diode to conduct from input to output, so anode at input, cathode at output. For P-MOS, body diode anode is drain, cathode is source. So drain should be input, source output. That matches: drain USBC_VBUS_IN, source +5V. So it's correct. Good.
